Miss Wallace (reel)

From the fiddle and flute duet playing of Kevin Moloney and Sean Moloney. Kevin was one of the original members of Ballinakill Traditional Players together with his father Stephen Moloney and Tommy Whelan. Sean is Kevin’s nephew and a son of legendary E. Galway flute player, Eddie Moloney.

On their recording, this tune is played with Miss Johnson and Miss Thornton.

This version is slightly different from the one in O’Neill’s. There are several similar tunes, notably Micho Russell’s (aka Sean Reid’s Fancy): https://thesession.org/tunes/2509

Composed by Paddy Sweeney

According to the liner notes of Danish band Moving Cloud’s CD “Sweet Nyaa” this tune was composed by fiddle player Paddy Sweeney, who was a native of Powelsboro, a little place between Tubbercurry and Ballymote. The title of the tune refers to a natural phenomenon which occasionally occurs when water pressure causes part of a bog to move or slide.
That’s the first tune, the one in G, that was composed by him.

Frank Quinn recording 1924

Frank Quinn (1893-1964) of Greagh, Drumlish, Co. Longford recorded this tune on the fiddle in May 1924. It was the first tune in a set entitled “Miss Wallace’s Reel” (The second tune was a version of “Rakish Paddy”). He probably learned it from O‘Neill’s book where it appears under that title. I transcribed his version and it follows O’Neill’s version closely.

Re: The Moving Bog - Composer?

Was Paddy Sweeney (1894-1974) of Powelsboro the likely composer of this reel? He would have been 9 years old when O‘Neill’s The Music of Ireland was published (with Miss Wallace #1452). Furthermore O’Neill took a version of the tune (The Wallace Twins, #298 in WSGM) from the Rice-Walsh manuscript. Rice collected the reel from the blind North Kerry fiddler Jeremiah Breen (b.1839) a nineteenth century musician.

↳ Posted by brailsford on January 19th, 2024.

Re: The Moving Bog

I think that whilst O‘Neill made something very worthwhile, there are numerous incorrect entries, but what matters is that there is good music in that book. I think that sometimes poeple make honest mistakes, and that at other times people embellish the truth to suit their own world view. A person can also want something so much that they’ll even make themselves believe it, no matter what. It may start of as a fanciful notion, but over a long period it can become a more concrete truth to oneself. Certainly, there are tunes in the book that aren’t even Irish, but O’Neill attributes them to Ireland, or to an Irish composer (e.g. George Brabazon, which is actually a Scots tune). Why? I guess he just wanted them to be Irish because they’re good, or maybe they’d been absorbed into the Irish tradition for long enough that he just assumed they were Irish…who knows? I don’t think it matters too much. It is, after all, a book of music and not one of historical facts. Just my thoughts on it…..

↳ Posted by Sesh on January 19th, 2024.
